opening: Mr. Chief Justice, and may it please the Court: The plurality and the concurrence in Freeman recognized two ways that a sentence following a C-type agreement can be based on the guidelines. Both are correct. Now those opinions differed in their reasoning, such that Freeman itself has no precedential effect under Marks, but the two approaches can be united under a common umbrella, namely, long-standing principles of proximate and multiple causation. And that's because each form of guidelines reliance bears a close connection to the sentence. The first --

Mr. Shumsky, could you address one issue for me on this question? In a (C) agreement, the government is giving up, often, certain things. Sometimes they dismiss additional charges. Sometimes, as here, they give up filing a persistent felony certificate. Sometimes they agree not to prosecute someone important to the defendant. There are many things that go into that bargain. How is a district court judge to determine whether a departure from the guideline range is justified? In what circumstances is what the government given up valuable enough to keep the original deal and when is it not?

Justice Sotomayor, let me answer the question in two parts if I can. First of all, those conditions, the way Your Honor describes C-type agreements, are true also for B-type agreements and for the sort of C-type agreements that the government concedes open the door to eligibility for relief under 3582(c)(2). So this particular category of C-type agreement that the government is proposing to carve out is not different in that way than all of these other categories of agreements. This --

Except that -- let's take -- dismissing charges, I -- I think it could be seen as relatively easy. How different were the charges and the exposure from what was kept and what was the strength of the government's evidence? And the government could talk about that at sentencing on those charges. But the persistent felony offender certificate is a different judgment, which is: I, the government, think that a sentence of X amount justifies giving up that certificate. How would a district court make up for the loss of that belief by the government?

opening: Justice Kennedy has the opinion of the court in Case 17-155, Hughes v. United States.

A Federal statute provides that in certain instances a prisoner who is serving a sentence is eligible for a sentence reduction when the Sentencing Commission has lowered the sentencing guidelines. The eligibility extends to a prisoner who has been sentenced to a term of imprisonment based on a sentencing range that has subsequently been lowered by the Sentencing Commission, and that statute is 18 U .S .C. Section 3582C2. The question here is whether the sentence imposed on the prisoner in this case was based on the guidelines when he enters his guilty plea under an agreement with the prosecution that is called a Type C plea agreement. And that's where the defendant and the government agree that the defendant will plead guilty and then serve a particular sentence, and the Type C agreement that they agree on must be then approved by the trial judge. Seven terms ago, in Freeman v. United States, this Court considered the same question that's involved here. That is, whether the sentence under a Type C agreement is based on the guidelines. In Freeman, no single interpretation or rationale commanded a majority of this Court. Now, Marx v. United States was the case decided in 1977, and Marx discussed what other courts should do when this Court has separate opinions addressing an issue, but when no single rationale commands a majority. So when confronted with the separate opinions on the sentencing question presented in Freeman, various courts of appeals consulted Marx to determine which Freeman opinion to follow, and they reached different conclusions. And in today's case, the Court had asked the parties to address the Marx question as a threshold issue. After consideration of the sentencing issue first discussed in Freeman, and now presented again here, the Court in today's case now has a majority with respect to that substantive sentencing issue. full_text: Justice Kennedy has the opinion of the court in Case 17-155, Hughes v. United States.

A Federal statute provides that in certain instances a prisoner who is serving a sentence is eligible for a sentence reduction when the Sentencing Commission has lowered the sentencing guidelines. The eligibility extends to a prisoner who has been sentenced to a term of imprisonment based on a sentencing range that has subsequently been lowered by the Sentencing Commission, and that statute is 18 U .S .C. Section 3582C2. The question here is whether the sentence imposed on the prisoner in this case was based on the guidelines when he enters his guilty plea under an agreement with the prosecution that is called a Type C plea agreement. And that's where the defendant and the government agree that the defendant will plead guilty and then serve a particular sentence, and the Type C agreement that they agree on must be then approved by the trial judge. Seven terms ago, in Freeman v. United States, this Court considered the same question that's involved here. That is, whether the sentence under a Type C agreement is based on the guidelines. In Freeman, no single interpretation or rationale commanded a majority of this Court. Now, Marx v. United States was the case decided in 1977, and Marx discussed what other courts should do when this Court has separate opinions addressing an issue, but when no single rationale commands a majority. So when confronted with the separate opinions on the sentencing question presented in Freeman, various courts of appeals consulted Marx to determine which Freeman opinion to follow, and they reached different conclusions. And in today's case, the Court had asked the parties to address the Marx question as a threshold issue. After consideration of the sentencing issue first discussed in Freeman, and now presented again here, the Court in today's case now has a majority with respect to that substantive sentencing issue. So it's unnecessary to discuss how Marx should be interpreted. The Court holds that a defendant who entered a Type C agreement is eligible for a sentence reduction under 3582c so long as the defendant's sentencing range was part of the framework the district court used in imposing the sentence or accepting the agreement. In the typical sentencing case, there will be no question that the defendant's guideline range was a basis for its sentence, for the guidelines are the starting point for every sentencing calculation in the Federal system. A sentence imposed pursuant to a Type C agreement is no exception to this general rule, although the government and the defendant may agree to a specific sentence. That bargain is contingent on the district courts accepting the agreement, and the guidelines prohibit courts from accepting a Type C agreement without first evaluating the recommended sentence in light of the defendant's guideline range. So in the usual case, the sentence imposed pursuant to the agreement is based on the defendant's guideline range. This interpretation furthers the purposes of the Sentencing Act. The Act aims to create a comprehensive sentencing scheme in which those who commit crimes of similar severity under similar conditions receive similar sentences. In this case, the district court accepted Petitioner Eric Hughes's Type C agreement, and it imposed a 180-month sentence after concluding that the sentence was consistent with the guidelines. Thus, the guideline range was a basis for the sentence that the district court imposed. That range has subsequently been lowered by the Sentencing Commission, so Hughes is eligible for relief under the section. The Court expresses no view as to whether the district court should exercise its discretion to reduce Hughes's sentence after considering the relevant statutory factors and the commission's policy statements. The judgment of the court of appeals is reversed. The case is remanded for further proceedings consistent with this opinion. Justice Sotomayor has filed a concurring opinion. The Chief Justice has filed a dissenting opinion in which Justices Thomas and Alito have joined.
